download-and-verify-a-release.text: You have cloned nothing. You want to know that a Singular release is what it says it is before you run it: that the files you downloaded are the files that were published, that the release names the formal model its evidence was checked against, and that the singular and open-datum commands of the release actually run a registry from creation to termination. One command answers all three, from the downloaded bytes alone, and either passes or refuses by name.

what-you-run.text: You need Nix with flakes enabled, on Linux: the verifier is built for x86_64-linux and aarch64-linux only, and it does not run on macOS. Nothing else: no checkout, no credentials, no running node.

The example names v0.12.0; the newest release is always at https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/releases/latest, and its tag goes in both places. Name the release you are checking twice: once to choose the verifier that release ships, once as the release to download. The verifier downloads the release's published assets from its GitHub release page without logging in:

The archive is unpacked into a fresh temporary directory, never inside a checkout. Pass --work DIR to choose that directory and keep what it leaves behind: the downloaded assets, the extracted archive and the receipts of every command the journey ran.

what-it-checks-in-order.text: Each check runs only when the ones before it passed, and the first one that fails ends the run with one line naming why.

The model revision is the commit of the application model, the formal specification the conformance evidence reads its statements at. The release states it in the archive as MODEL-REVISION; the verifier compares it with the revision the conformance evidence of the same release is compiled against. A release that ships bundles has each platform's bundle checked against the commit its tag names, and the bundle of your platform is run. The journey is the registration journey of the release: a registry is created, keys are registered, folded, updated and terminated, read back and folded in a discovered batch, each command a separate singular or open-datum process on one development network the verifier starts and stops itself. Every verdict is computed from the chain's own record or from files, and none is typed; create, register, update, terminate, read and the discovered batch fold are each judged from the chain's record and shown failing on altered input. The journey plays the bundle of your platform: its commands, its blueprint and its development node, none of them built on your machine. A release before the bundles, a release read with --without-bundles, and a platform that has no bundle play the commands built from the archive's own flakes.

Before starting the journey, the verifier strips and inspects the actual compiled singular and open-datum executables built from the archive and reads their resolved registry CLI build flags. Both must exclude hidden test inputs and disable the test flag. It then records every ordinary journey invocation: every singular and open-datum command the journey runs, inspect and submit included, must run without hidden harness inputs, and no hold marker may appear.

Fault injection, crash recovery, race controls and independent trie-capability observations run in the explicit test build. Their unchanged assertions are separate required CI evidence. They do not claim to have run inside these extracted release binaries.

what-a-refusal-means.text: A refusal is one line, verify-release: REFUSED <name>: <detail>, and the exit status is 1.
A release that passes prints its tag, both archive checksums, the model revision and the directory it was verified in.
